title: WHY WAS INCEST HAPPENING INSIDE THE CORINTHIAN CHURCH?
paragraphs:
WHY WAS INCEST HAPPENING INSIDE THE CORINTHIAN CHURCH?
The scandal was horrifying. But what Paul confronted next may be even more frightening—because the greatest danger was not simply what one man was doing in secret, but what an entire church had learned to tolerate in the name of belonging.
Imagine walking into church on Sunday.
People are talking.
Someone is praying.
Someone is quoting Scripture.
Someone is probably convinced that this congregation understands grace better than everybody else.
And somewhere in that gathering sits a man whose relationship has become so scandalous that Paul says even the surrounding pagan culture would recognize something was terribly wrong.
Yet the church is still functioning.
People are still gathering.
People are still talking about spiritual things.
And apparently, somehow, they have learned to live with it.
Then a letter arrives.
Paul has heard.
And the opening words of 1 Corinthians 5 land like a thunderclap:
“Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία…”
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia…
“It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you…”
Then Paul becomes painfully specific.
“…ὥστε γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν.”
…hōste gynaika tina tou patros echein.
Literally, the horrifying situation involved a man “having” his father’s wife.
Paul does not say “his mother.”
He says “his father’s wife.”
That distinction matters.

The wording most naturally suggests that the woman was the man’s stepmother, although Paul does not give us enough information to reconstruct every detail of the relationship. We are not told whether the father was dead, divorced, separated, or otherwise absent from the situation. Scripture does not tell us, so we should not pretend that it does.
But Scripture tells us enough.
This relationship violated a boundary God had already made unmistakably clear.

Leviticus 18:8 forbade uncovering the nakedness of one’s father’s wife. Leviticus 20:11 condemns sexual relations with one’s father’s wife. Deuteronomy 27:20 pronounces a curse upon the one who lies with his father’s wife because he has dishonored his father’s bed.
Paul was not inventing a new Christian sexual ethic because Corinth made him uncomfortable.
He was confronting behavior that stood against the moral boundaries already revealed in Scripture.
And there is something else we need to understand before turning Corinth into a convenient story about “those terrible ancient people.”
Paul's Greek word is πορνεία—porneia.
Sexual immorality.
But Paul's outrage is not directed only toward the man committing it.
Read the next sentence and suddenly the spotlight moves.
“And you are proud!”
That is where this passage becomes uncomfortable.
Because Paul does not merely ask:
How could this man do this?
Paul effectively asks:
How could the church become comfortable while this was happening?
That question survived Corinth.
It walked through twenty centuries of church history.
And now it is standing in front of us.
Because the terrifying lesson of Corinth is not simply that terrible sin can enter a church.
We already know that.
Churches are filled with sinners because there is no other kind of human being available.
The terrifying lesson is that people can become so confused about grace, freedom, love, acceptance, status, spirituality, or tolerance that they stop grieving over what is destroying someone.
There is a difference between welcoming sinners and celebrating bondage.
There is a difference between showing mercy and renaming darkness.
There is a difference between refusing self-righteous condemnation and refusing biblical discernment.
Jesus ate with sinners.
Jesus loved sinners.
Jesus touched people religious society avoided.
Jesus defended the broken.
Jesus received the ashamed.
And Jesus called people to repentance.
Those truths do not fight each other.
They meet at the cross.
That is where Corinth had to be brought.
And that is where we have to be brought too.
Because perhaps the question beneath the scandal is not merely, “Why was incest happening inside the Corinthian church?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
Why had the church stopped mourning?
Paul tells them they should have grieved.
That word changes the atmosphere completely.
Christian holiness is not supposed to sound like a mob celebrating the destruction of somebody caught in sin.
It sounds like mourning.
It sounds like a family watching someone they love walk toward a cliff.
It sounds like tears.
It sounds like, “Brother, this is killing you.”
It sounds like, “Sister, Jesus has something better than this.”
It sounds like someone loving you enough to refuse to applaud while chains are wrapping themselves around your soul.
Biblical correction without love becomes cruelty.
But what our generation desperately needs to understand is that love without truth can become cruelty too.
If someone is walking toward destruction, silence is not always kindness.
Sometimes silence is abandonment wearing a smile.
And Corinth had apparently become dangerously comfortable.
Paul writes:
Then he gives them an image almost anybody in the ancient world could understand.
A little leaven works through the whole lump.
Sin rarely stays politely inside the boundaries we assign to it.
What we excuse begins teaching us.
What we repeatedly tolerate begins reshaping our conscience.
What once made us tremble eventually becomes ordinary.
The first compromise feels enormous.
The fiftieth barely registers.
That is how spiritual numbness works.
Nobody usually wakes up one morning and announces, “Today I will destroy my conscience.”
It happens slowly.
One justification.
One hidden browser window.
One secret conversation.
One flirtation.
One dishonest transaction.
One bitterness we refuse to surrender.
One addiction we keep renaming.
One relationship we know dishonors Christ but cannot imagine releasing.
One compromise followed by another.
And eventually we become capable of sitting peacefully beside something that once would have driven us to our knees.
Maybe that is why this chapter makes us uncomfortable.
We want to stare at Corinth's scandal.
Paul wants us to examine our own tolerance.
You may never commit the particular sin described in 1 Corinthians 5.
But you can still become Corinthian in the way you protect the thing Jesus is asking you to surrender.
We all know how to rename our favorite sins.
Greed becomes ambition.
Gossip becomes concern.
Lust becomes loneliness.
Bitterness becomes discernment.
Pride becomes confidence.
Cowardice becomes keeping the peace.
Materialism becomes “God's blessing.”
Unforgiveness becomes boundaries even when what we actually mean is revenge.
Compromise becomes complexity.
And sometimes rebellion simply becomes, “God understands.”
Yes.
God understands.
Far more deeply than we do.
He understands the wound beneath the behavior.
He understands the loneliness.
He understands the childhood.
He understands the trauma.
He understands the temptation.
He understands the nights nobody saw.
He understands why you reached for something that promised relief.
He understands every tear.
Every failure.
Every rationalization.
Every relapse.
Every secret.
And because He understands completely, He also understands exactly what that sin is doing to you.
Grace does not mean God finally decides sin does not matter.
Grace means sin mattered so much that Jesus Christ carried its judgment upon Himself so sinners could be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, and transformed.
That is why Paul's response to Corinth sounds severe.
He commands the church to remove the unrepentant man from their fellowship.
But even here, the purpose is not merely humiliation.
Paul's stated horizon is ultimately redemptive: “…so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”
Do not miss that.
Even discipline has salvation in view.
Even confrontation has restoration in view.
Even the painful removal of false security is meant to awaken someone before destruction becomes permanent.
Biblical church discipline is not supposed to be revenge.
It is not entertainment.
It is not gossip dressed like discernment.
It is not an opportunity for spiritually proud people to feel cleaner because somebody else's sin became public.
It is a desperate refusal to tell someone that everything is fine when everything is not fine.
Because Jesus loves sinners too much to make peace with the thing enslaving them.
And then Paul does something breathtaking.
In the middle of a chapter about sexual scandal, discipline, corruption, and judgment, he suddenly points toward a Lamb.
“For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.”
There.
That is the center.
Not Corinth.
Not incest.
Not scandal.
Christ.
The answer to human corruption is not merely stronger embarrassment.
The answer is Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
Our Passover Lamb has been sacrificed.
The blood has been shed.
The price has been paid.
The door of mercy is open.
And that means the person reading this with a secret does not need to run farther into darkness.
You can come home.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been doing.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
Maybe you lead.
Maybe you preach.
Maybe you serve.
Maybe you post Bible verses while fighting something privately that would shock the people who follow you.
Maybe your scandal has never become public.
But heaven does not need screenshots.
God already knows.
And strangely enough, that may be the most comforting sentence you read today.
God already knows.
And He is still calling you.
Not toward excuses.
Toward repentance.
Not toward hiding.
Toward light.
Not toward pretending.
Toward confession.
Not toward self-destruction.
Toward Christ.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing outside your locked room waiting for you to clean everything before He enters.
The Gospel is Jesus coming for sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
But when grace finds us, grace does not leave us chained to the same grave.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
This is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace finally convinces us that coming home is better than staying hidden.
Maybe this article stopped being about an unnamed man in ancient Corinth several paragraphs ago.
Maybe now it is about you.
The affair nobody knows about.
The pornography.
The secret messages.
The hatred.
The money.
The dishonesty.
The double life.
The addiction.
The relationship.
The compromise.
The pride.
The resentment you feed whenever their name appears.
The private version of yourself you desperately hope never becomes public.
Listen carefully.
Your greatest danger may not be that somebody discovers your scandal.
Your greatest danger may be becoming comfortable enough with it that you no longer want freedom.
That is what makes Corinth frightening.
They had apparently learned to coexist with what should have made them mourn.
Do not wait until your chains feel normal.
Bring them to Jesus.
Not because you are beyond grace.
Because grace is exactly why you can stop hiding.
There is no repentance so deep that Christ's mercy becomes shallow.
There is no confession that surprises the One who already carried our sins to Calvary.
There is no stain that becomes stronger than the blood of Christ.
But grace must never become permission to protect what nailed our Savior to the cross.
Grace opens the prison door.
Repentance walks out.
And Jesus calls us into freedom.
So perhaps you need to do something after reading this.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you feel more spiritual.
Today.
Tell God the truth.
If another person needs to know, seek wise, biblically faithful help and bring what has been hidden into appropriate light.
If someone has been harmed, repentance includes taking responsibility rather than manipulating them into instant reconciliation.
If you need pastoral accountability, pursue it.
If you are trapped in habitual sexual sin, stop treating isolation as strength.

And if what happened to you involved abuse, coercion, exploitation, or victimization, understand this clearly: being sinned against is not the same thing as committing the sin described in 1 Corinthians 5. Do not carry another person's guilt as though it were yours.
The cross exposes evil without confusing the wounded with the one who wounded them.
And the cross offers mercy to sinners who truly turn to Christ.
That is the strange beauty hidden inside this horrifying chapter.
Scandal does not have to write the final sentence.
Jesus does.
Peter's denial did not write his final sentence.
The Samaritan woman's past did not write hers.
The thief's crimes did not get the last word beside the cross.
Paul's persecution of Christians did not become the final chapter of his life.
And your worst chapter does not have authority to finish your story if your story is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
From scandal...
to confession.
From confession...
to repentance.
From repentance...
to grace.
From grace...
to restoration.
From restoration...
to a life that becomes evidence that Jesus still rewrites people.
Maybe someone you know is hiding right now.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Send it privately to the believer who thinks failure means Jesus no longer wants them.
And if this exposed something hidden, you do not owe strangers the intimate details of your life. But you can simply comment, “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There are people reading who need to discover that they are not the only ones fighting.
That is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture outrage.
Not to build a platform around other people's failures.
But to keep bringing wounded, wandering, compromised, hungry people back to Scripture...
back to repentance...
back to grace...
back to the cross...
back to Jesus Christ.
We glorify God ultimately through lives surrendered to Christ.

If you want deeper biblical nourishment, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, accountability, and Christ-centered teaching that refuses both loveless condemnation and comfortable compromise, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person who walked away from church.
Invite the skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing to say to broken people.
Invite the person whose life looks perfect online and is collapsing behind the screen.
Because somewhere tonight, someone may be staring at a secret and wondering whether their story is already over.
Tell them it isn't.
Tell them Corinth was scandalous.
Tell them the church had failed.
Tell them sin was confronted.
Tell them repentance mattered.
Tell them grace was not cheap.
Tell them Christ had been sacrificed.
Tell them there is still a road home.
And before you leave this page, remember the sentence the enemy desperately hopes you will forget:
Your scandal may explain the chapter you are standing in, but surrendered to Christ, it does not get to write the ending.
